title: How I Edit a Travel Vlog in 30 Minutes (Real Time)
creator: Jun Park
description:
200 clips from a weekend in Kyoto, edited start to finish against a timer. My whole process, step by step.

Music: licensed lo-fi track
Shot on a phone + a small action cam, flat profile

The finished Kyoto vlog goes up Friday.

sentences.t: I filmed a weekend in Kyoto last month, and I came home with about two hundred clips and zero energy to edit them.
So today I'm going to edit the whole vlog in thirty minutes, and I'll show you every step.
Timer is going, starting now.
Step one happens before I open any software.
I go through the clips on my computer and delete anything that's obviously bad, blurry, or my thumb over the lens.
Then I drop the rest into three folders, morning, afternoon, and night.
That takes about five minutes, and it saves me so much scrolling later.
Okay, time to edit.
I'm cutting this one in Clipforge, and quick note, they're sponsoring this tutorial, so thanks to them.
I drag all three folders into a new project, and it keeps them as bins, so my morning, afternoon and night stuff stays separate.
First pass is the rough cut.
I skim through each clip with the hover preview, hit I and O to mark the good part, then press E to drop it on the end of the timeline.
I'm not thinking about music or color yet, just story, so I'm going roughly in the order things happened.
The fox shrine at sunrise, the train, the market, the bamboo forest, dinner, and the walk back.
Twelve minutes in, and I have a rough cut that's about six minutes long, which is too long.
Second pass, I tighten.
I'm turning on silence detection for my talking clips, and it highlights every pause longer than half a second.
I go through them one by one rather than deleting all of them, because some pauses are actually doing something, like right after I see the view.
Now, music.
I've got a lo-fi track I already licensed, so I drop it under everything, then turn on beat markers so I can see where the drums hit.
Then I nudge my cuts so the scene changes land on the beat, especially in the market montage, because that's what makes it feel edited and not just stuck together.
Color next, and I keep this really simple.
I shot everything in a flat profile, so I apply one base grade to the whole timeline, a little contrast, warmer highlights, and that's ninety percent of it.
The night clips are too noisy, so I select just those and add a bit of noise reduction.
Last, captions.
I hit auto-caption, it transcribes all my talking bits, and I fix the two places where it heard Kyoto as Tokyo, which, fair.
Then I pick a simple white style with a soft shadow and apply it to all of them at once.
And, time.
Twenty-eight minutes and forty seconds.
Is it the best vlog I've ever made?
No.
But it's done, and done is so much better than two hundred clips sitting on a hard drive for a year.
A couple of things I want you to take from this.
One, sort your footage before you edit, even if it's just three folders.
Two, rough cut for story first, and only then worry about music and color.
Three, set a timer, because editing will happily eat your whole weekend if you let it.
And four, the first version doesn't have to be perfect, you can always make a long version later.
I'll put the finished Kyoto vlog up on Friday, so you can see how it turned out.
Let me know how long your edits usually take in the comments, and I'll see you next time.
